strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/bacc81ca51474a6c8b3fea5d7b5544ac/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important practical problem: scaling video-language models to long, information-dense videos without irreversible token pruning.

VideoNSA provides a sensible video-specific adaptation of Native Sparse Attention, combining frame-aligned compression, content-dependent block selection, local attention, and dense attention for text.

The evaluation spans six benchmarks covering long-video, temporal, and spatial reasoning. Against the reported same-backbone alternatives, VideoNSA is strongest on four benchmarks and particularly improves Tomato and very-long-duration TimeScope subsets.
The paper includes useful analyses of context allocation, attention allocation, branch gates, and attention sinks, and compares against a dense model fine-tuned on the same data.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is insufficiently validated. There is no end-to-end latency, throughput, peak-memory, or training-efficiency comparison against dense attention or competing sparse/compression methods. Figure 6 only decomposes VideoNSA's own branch latency and omits hardware, batch-size, precision, and measurement details.

The claimed 3.6% attention budget appears under-specified and potentially misleading. The formula counts selected blocks and the sliding window but seemingly omits the compression branch, the cost of three separate attention operations, gating, and the quadratic block-selection scoring cost. The paper itself states that selection has O(L^2/b) complexity and compression dominates runtime, weakening the claimed near-linear scalability.

Novelty is limited: the three-branch learnable mechanism and gating are inherited directly from NSA. The principal additions are its application to video tokens, frame-aligned blocking, and modality-dependent use of NSA versus GQA; the paper does not clearly isolate which of these adaptations is technically essential.

Accuracy comparisons are not fully controlled. VideoNSA receives expensive end-to-end training (4600 H100 GPU-hours), whereas most competing sparse and compression baselines are training-free. There is no comparably trained sparse-attention baseline or accuracy-versus-realized-latency comparison, so the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed architecture.

The branch-removal ablations are difficult to interpret. Gates use independent sigmoid outputs rather than normalized mixture weights, so disabling branches changes output magnitude as well as information pathways. The severe degradation therefore does not establish that all three branches are complementary; retrained ablations or gate renormalization are needed.

Reported gains are generally modest and lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. There are also numerical inconsistencies across tables, such as LongVideoBench being 60.0 in Table 1 versus 60.2 in Table 7 and VSIBench being 36.1 versus 36.0.

Reproducibility is presently weak: the project, code, and model links are blank; important implementation details of selection scoring, hybrid attention masks, kernel configuration, and latency measurement are missing. The ethics statement also asserts privacy compliance, safeguards, and bias mitigation without reporting concrete audits.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: scaling multimodal language models to long videos without discarding visual tokens.
The adaptation of Native Sparse Attention to a hybrid video/text setting is technically plausible, and retaining dense attention for text is a sensible design choice.
Evaluation spans six benchmarks covering long-video, temporal, and spatial reasoning, with comparisons against dense, token-compression, and training-free sparse-attention baselines.
The paper includes useful exploratory analyses of context allocation, attention budgets, branch behavior, and attention sinks.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited: the compression, selection, sliding-window, and gating mechanisms are largely inherited from Native Sparse Attention. The main contribution is an application and training recipe for video-language models rather than a substantially new attention method.

The central efficiency claims are inadequately supported. There is no end-to-end latency, throughput, peak-memory, or training-efficiency comparison against dense attention and other sparse baselines. Figure 6 only decomposes VideoNSA's branch latency, without reporting hardware, batch size, repetitions, variability, or a dense reference.

The claimed near-linear scaling is questionable because the paper itself states that selection-score computation costs O(L^2/b). Reporting that only 3.6% of dense attention edges are used does not establish equivalent wall-clock or memory savings, especially given kernel and selection overhead.

Accuracy gains over the strongest sparse baselines are modest or inconsistent: VideoNSA ties MInference on LongTimeScope, trails MInference/XAttention on VSIBench, and improves several other benchmarks by small margins. No confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests are provided, so it is unclear which differences are meaningful.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently controlled. VideoNSA receives expensive end-to-end training, whereas most competing efficient methods are applied training-free. Dense-SFT is useful but degrades on several tasks, and the study does not compare against a similarly trained alternative sparse architecture or isolate gains from sparse attention versus architecture-specific optimization.

The branch ablation is difficult to interpret. Removing branches only at inference from a jointly trained, independently sigmoid-gated model can change output magnitude and create distribution shift; the dramatic degradation therefore does not demonstrate that all three branches are intrinsically necessary. Retrained variants, normalized gates, or branch-dropout controls are needed.

Several claims exceed the evidence. The paper claims consistent superiority, hardware awareness, near-linear time and memory, and processing over 10,000 frames on one GPU, but does not provide the corresponding controlled measurements. The attention-sink analysis is observational and does not establish that lower sink counts cause better accuracy or that gating counteracts sinks.

There are notable reporting inconsistencies and errors: the maximum training context is described as both 36K and 32K; LongVideoBench scores vary across tables; Table 27 is labeled MLVU but contains Tomato categories and duplicates Table 28; and the project, code, and model links are blank.

Reproducibility is weak despite listing basic hyperparameters. The filtered training split, preprocessing details, exact implementation, evaluation prompts, hardware/kernel configuration, random seeds, and code/model artifacts are unavailable. Reproducing the reported 4,600 H100-GPU-hour training run would also be prohibitively expensive for many groups.

The ethics statement makes unsupported assertions that the public data comply with privacy regulations and that safeguards and bias evaluations were performed, without describing those checks or reporting results.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in long-video understanding and presents a practical adaptation of Native Sparse Attention to a strong multimodal backbone. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3e352a4277b94091915cac4297e4adb3/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The evaluation is broad, covering six benchmarks spanning long-form, temporal, and spatial understanding. VideoNSA improves over the dense Qwen2.5-VL baseline on every reported aggregate metric and is generally competitive with or better than same-backbone compression and sparse-attention baselines.
Including a dense model fine-tuned on the same data is valuable: its mostly negative results suggest that VideoNSA's gains are not explained solely by additional instruction tuning.

The paper provides substantial diagnostic analysis, including branch combinations, context and attention-budget allocation, gate behavior, branch latency, and attention sinks. These analyses offer useful practical insights beyond a leaderboard comparison.

The hybrid treatment of modalities—sparse attention for the long visual prefix while retaining dense attention for text—is sensible, and extrapolation from a 36K training context to evaluations reaching 128K is practically interesting.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is insufficiently demonstrated. The paper reports only per-branch latency for VideoNSA, without end-to-end latency, peak memory, throughput, FLOPs, hardware/batch details, or direct comparisons against FlashAttention and the competing sparse methods. Consequently, claims of hardware-aware, near-linear scalability and practical acceleration are not convincingly supported.

Novelty is limited: the three-branch mechanism is largely inherited from Native Sparse Attention, while the main methodological contribution is its modality-specific application and training on video data. The paper does not clearly isolate which video-specific design choices are technically new beyond frame-aligned blocks and hybrid visual/text attention.

Several scaling claims are stronger than the reported evidence. Performance is not consistently improved at longer contexts: for example, LongTimeScope, MLVU, and VSIBench contain 128K configurations that underperform shorter-context configurations. Thus, successful execution at 128K is shown, but reliable performance scaling to 128K across tasks is not.

The branch ablation protocol is unclear. If branches are removed only at inference from a jointly trained three-branch model, the severe degradation may primarily reflect distribution shift and does not establish that independently trained one- or two-branch alternatives are intrinsically inferior.

Reported headline values are inconsistent across tables—for example, LongVideoBench appears as 60.0, 60.2, and 59.4; TimeScope as 83.7 and 82.7; and Tomato as 26.5 and 26.2—without explaining configuration differences. Small improvements are also reported without uncertainty or repeated runs.

The comparison is asymmetric because VideoNSA receives expensive end-to-end training while most sparse and compression baselines are training-free. The dense-SFT control helps, but similarly trained sparse alternatives or an NSA baseline without the proposed video-specific choices would better establish architectural merit.

Some implementation details remain ambiguous: compression is variously described as a learned MLP and frame-token averaging, selection-score computation is largely deferred to prior work, and the attention-budget equation does not clearly account for all three branches. Blank code/model links further limit current reproducibility.

The attention-sink conclusions are mostly correlational. Attention distributions normalized over branches with different supports are not obviously directly comparable, and the claim that dynamic gating counteracts compression-induced sinks lacks a controlled causal ablation.

strengths: VideoNSA addresses an important bottleneck in long-video MLLMs by adapting learnable Native Sparse Attention to visual tokens while retaining dense grouped-query attention for text. The modality-specific hybrid design is sensible and practically relevant.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, spatial reasoning, and two additional benchmarks. VideoNSA generally improves over the dense base model and performs especially well on TimeScope, LongTimeScope, Tomato, and LSDBench.

The paper contains unusually extensive diagnostic analyses, including context and attention-budget scaling, branch combinations, static versus input-dependent gates, layer/head gate behavior, attention sinks, theoretical FLOPs, and measured latency.
The same-data dense fine-tuning control is useful: it suggests that the gains are not explained merely by instruction tuning, since dense SFT often degrades while VideoNSA improves.

The appendices provide training hyperparameters, evaluation configurations, subtask-level results, and implementation-related efficiency discussion, making the experimental setup more informative than the main paper alone.
weaknesses: The central efficiency claim is not fully convincing. The implemented VideoNSA requires 4.68 PFLOPs rather than the ideal 2.05 PFLOPs and is slower than FlashAttention in the reported latency plots at long contexts. No peak-memory, throughput, end-to-end generation latency, or accuracy-versus-latency comparison is provided, despite claims of hardware awareness, near-linear efficiency, and memory scalability.

Baseline fairness is limited: VideoNSA receives expensive end-to-end training (4600 H100 GPU-hours), whereas the principal sparse and compression baselines are training-free. Dense SFT is a valuable control, but equally trained sparse alternatives or fine-tuned versions of the strongest baselines are absent. Consequently, the gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed sparse architecture rather than architecture-specific training.

Many improvements are modest and no uncertainty, repeated-run variance, or significance analysis is reported. For example, gains on LongVideoBench and MLVU are around 0.6–1.3 points, while some strong sparse baselines match VideoNSA on LongTimeScope or outperform it on VSIBench. This weakens claims of consistent superiority.

The 128K scaling claim is overstated. Table 27 shows that VideoNSA peaks at 64K on MLVU, LongTimeScope, and VSIBench and declines at 128K; only LongVideoBench and TimeScope improve. Demonstrating that inference runs at 128K is not the same as establishing reliable performance scaling to 128K.

The branch-removal study appears to disable branches at inference without retraining the reduced models. The resulting severe degradation shows distribution shift relative to the trained three-branch model, but does not establish that every branch is intrinsically necessary or that the proposed combination is better than properly trained one- or two-branch alternatives.

The theoretical discussion of routing-path stability and RoPE is largely post hoc and unsupported by direct measurements of the defined routing deviation. Some premises, such as an effectively unchanged routing structure when sequence length and candidate evidence change, are not justified for content-dependent selection.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the project, code, and model fields are blank; important latency protocol details such as hardware, batch size, precision, warm-up, repetition count, and variability are missing; and dataset filtering is not specified sufficiently to recreate the exact 216K subset.

There are several consistency and presentation problems that reduce confidence in the results: headline scores vary across tables without adequate explanation, Table 31 is labeled MLVU but contains Tomato categories and duplicates Table 32, some configurations yield unexplained zero or near-random performance, and architectural notation such as the relationship between frame token count and the fixed block size is ambiguous.

The ethics statement asserts that bias mitigation and dataset safeguards were performed but provides no procedure or evidence. It also does not meaningfully discuss privacy, surveillance, or misuse risks specific to long-video understanding.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: scaling video-language models to long visual contexts without discarding input tokens.
The modality-specific design—sparse attention for video tokens while retaining dense attention for text—is intuitive and practically relevant.
Evaluation spans multiple long-video, temporal-reasoning, and spatial-understanding benchmarks, with additional studies of context length, attention allocation, latency, gates, and attention sinks.
VideoNSA obtains meaningful gains over the dense backbone on several tasks, especially LongTimeScope, Tomato, and VSIBench, and reports both theoretical FLOPs and wall-clock latency.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are overstated. VideoNSA is best on only some benchmarks, ties MInference on LongTimeScope, and trails MInference/XAttention on VSIBench. At 128K, performance decreases on MLVU, LongTimeScope, and VSIBench, contradicting claims of consistent improvement and reliable scaling.

The comparison is not fully fair: VideoNSA receives 4,600 H100-hours of end-to-end training, while most sparse and compression baselines are training-free. The dense SFT control degrades on most benchmarks because the authors acknowledge limited training-data quality, making it difficult to separate architectural benefits from training effects. Comparisons with other trainable multimodal sparse-attention methods are missing.

The branch ablation is not convincing. Branches appear to be disabled only at inference rather than retraining each architecture. Because three sigmoid-gated outputs are summed without normalization, removing branches changes both capacity and activation scale; the resulting degradation does not establish that all branches are intrinsically necessary.

Several reported results are internally inconsistent or erroneous. LongVideoBench is 60.0 in Table 1 but 60.2 in Table 7; Table 3 reports different VideoNSA values from Table 1 without clearly identifying the changed setting. Most seriously, the purported MLVU attention-budget results in Table 31 use Tomato's categories and are numerically duplicated in Table 32. Some configurations inexplicably produce exactly zero across all VSIBench or LongTimeScope categories. These problems materially reduce confidence in the evaluation.

No random seeds, repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance tests are provided. Many headline gains are only 0.6–1.3 points, so it is unclear whether they exceed evaluation variance or sensitivity to frame sampling.

The theoretical section is technically problematic. It represents an attention mask as elementwise multiplication with the query, Q⊙M', although sequence masks operate on query-key logits and generally have incompatible dimensions with Q. It also assumes the routing mask remains unchanged during context scaling despite content-dependent selection, and the RoPE and routing-stability explanations are speculative rather than demonstrated empirically.

The efficiency evidence does not support the strongest framing. Selection remains quadratic in sequence length up to the block factor, practical VideoNSA FLOPs are over twice the ideal estimate, and VideoNSA is slower than several training-free sparse baselines in the reported 128K latency comparison. Memory consumption, decoding throughput, batch-size effects, and precise measurement protocol/hardware are not adequately reported.

The attention-sink analysis is under-specified and largely correlational. The normalization of the received-attention threshold is unclear, scores from structurally different branches may not be directly comparable, and no intervention demonstrates that the measured sinks harm performance or that gating causally mitigates them.

Reproducibility is weak: the project, code, and model links are blank; important implementation details such as selection-score computation and latency protocol are incomplete; and reproducing training requires thousands of H100-hours.

The manuscript contains many presentation and quality-control issues, including malformed prose, typographical errors, crowded appendix tables, inconsistent terminology, and an unsupported boilerplate ethics statement claiming privacy compliance, bias mitigation, and dataset safeguards without describing any audit or evidence.

strengths: VideoNSA is a clear and practically relevant adaptation of learnable Native Sparse Attention to video-language models, combining compression, selection, and sliding-window branches while retaining dense attention for text tokens.

The evaluation is broad: six principal benchmarks cover long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial understanding, with two additional benchmarks in the appendix. Comparisons include dense Qwen2.5-VL, a same-data dense SFT baseline, token-compression methods, and several sparse-attention baselines.

Results provide concrete positive evidence of competitiveness. VideoNSA is best or near-best across the main benchmarks, with especially meaningful gains on LongTimeScope, Tomato, and VSIBench, while improving practical long-context efficiency over dense attention.

The paper contains unusually extensive analyses of context allocation, attention budgets, branch combinations, dynamic versus static gating, latency, FLOPs, and attention behavior. The static-gate ablation offers useful evidence that input-dependent routing matters.

The manuscript is generally well organized, and the architecture, training recipe, evaluation settings, and major implementation constraints are documented in substantial detail. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3dcd4dba2acf456b9ec113e9860c42a6/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is moderate: the three-branch mechanism is inherited largely from NSA, and the primary innovation is its modality-specific adaptation and empirical investigation rather than a fundamentally new sparse-attention method.

The headline comparison is not entirely controlled because VideoNSA receives expensive end-to-end training whereas most sparse and compression baselines are training-free. The same-data dense SFT baseline helps, but trained versions of competing sparse architectures or a matched-compute comparison would better isolate the architectural advantage.

Some claims are stronger than the reported evidence. In particular, the claim of consistently improving up to 128K conflicts with Table 27, where performance from 64K to 128K decreases on MLVU, LongTimeScope, and VSIBench. The near-linear characterization also needs qualification because the selection branch retains a quadratic component.

The practical efficiency advantage is less compelling than the framing suggests. VideoNSA uses 0.56 times the dense FLOPs and reaches 3.1 times speedup at 128K, while several training-free sparse baselines reach roughly 4.1 times; the current kernel's head padding and compression overhead substantially reduce the theoretical hardware advantage. Attention-budget accounting should also state clearly whether every branch, particularly compression, is included in the reported 3.6 percent.

The branch-removal ablation appears to disable branches at inference rather than retrain matched variants, so its large degradation does not by itself establish that every branch is intrinsically necessary. The attention-sink analysis is descriptive and does not establish that reduced sink ratios cause the accuracy gains.

There are presentation and reproducibility issues: no uncertainty estimates or repeated-run analysis are reported despite several sub-point improvements; some headline values differ across tables; Table 31 appears mislabeled or duplicated from the Tomato results; and the project, code, and model links are blank. Reproduction would also be expensive at the reported 4600 H100 GPU-hours.
